Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A man in his 60s has longstanding asthma, nasal polyps, sinus disease and previous eosinophilia up to 3.8×10^9/L. ANCA was negative and earlier biopsies did not show vasculitis. A clinical diagnosis of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis had been made. Mepolizumab controlled symptoms for five years; he stopped it two years ago.
Asthma and sinus symptoms returned over the past year. He developed right facial pain seven months ago, steroid-responsive bilateral facial weakness five months ago and painful right visual loss three months ago. Vision improved after prednisone and doxycycline, without establishing which intervention explained it.
Following a prednisone reduction from 30 to 20 mg, right V2 pain and sensory loss persisted. An outside MRI reading emphasised small-vessel and sinus changes; institutional review describes multifocal dural enhancement. Later symptoms, cardiac tests and treatment response are not supplied.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the evolving neurological problem and compare up to three explanations. Explain how the historical disease label, negative tests, steroid response and revised imaging should influence a provisional assessment and urgent further review. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "**Provisional Assessment and Urgent Review**

Observed facts: A man in his 60s with longstanding asthma, nasal polyps, sinus disease, and eosinophilia (peak 3.8×10⁹/L) carries a clinical EGPA label despite negative ANCA and biopsies without vasculitis. After stopping mepolizumab, he developed sequential cranial neuropathies (right V2, bilateral facial, right optic) with steroid-responsive visual loss and persistent V2 sensory loss on prednisone 20 mg. Institutional MRI review identifies multifocal dural enhancement, superseding an outside reading of small-vessel and sinus changes.

Hypotheses to compare:

1. EGPA with pachymeningitis: Dural enhancement and cranial neuropathy fit EGPA, but negative ANCA and absent vasculitis on prior biopsy weaken tissue confirmation. The label remains a working diagnosis, not a proven one.

2. IgG4-related disease: Causes pachymeningitis, cranial neuropathies, and is steroid-responsive. It can coexist with or mimic EGPA and would explain steroid dependence with relapse on taper.

3. Chronic granulomatous infection: Doxycycline response is ambiguous, but steroid-responsive visual loss could mask an indolent infection, particularly with immunosuppression.

Proposed actions: Urgent review should include serum IgG4, repeat imaging with contrast, consideration of dural biopsy if accessible, and infectious workup before escalating immunosuppression. An essential requirement is one whose omission materially compromises the assessment or decision required by the task. Its relevance must be justified by the presentation available at that point, not by hindsight from a hidden result or later outcome.
